evidence: Not a defect claim: the reviewer affirms that the README's new default-prompt wording matches the collector-based flow, and the round-0 review was DISMISSED with no must-change item. Nothing in README.md needed changing and nothing was changed.

The reviewer blesses buildPatchAnchors as 'consistent with GitHub review API semantics', and it is right that GitHub counts context lines; but the code skipped EVERY @@ header rather than only the first, an off-by-N on multi-hunk patches that this affirmation missed and that round 2 later reached from a wrong premise (F16).
guidance_note: pin an external numbering protocol to its spec, not to the shape of a single-hunk example, before shipping the anchor table.

evidence: Another affirmation, not a finding: the README text does match submitCleanReview, which prints APPROVED_MESSAGE regardless of whether a formal review was submitted. No action was owed.

At the merge commit 28b275f, core.info(APPROVED_MESSAGE) still sits outside if (canApprove), and the README the same PR ships says 'In either case, if there are no findings, it will print an approval message' - the unconditional print is documented intent, so [LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow] is pasted onto a log-line preference. The thread was resolved with no reply and no change.
guidance_note: put the intent of a deliberately unconditional log on the line itself, so a reviewer reading only the function cannot read intent as an oversight.

evidence: F5 asks to move the log INSIDE if (canApprove) while F4, on the same line in the same round, asks to log only when submission is skipped - directly contradictory instructions for one line. Neither was applied; the line is unchanged at 28b275f.
guidance_note: when one round emits two findings that contradict each other on one line, answer both threads with the contradiction named; leaving both silent hides that the reviewer disagreed with itself.

evidence: Byte-for-byte the same claim as F4, raised against dist/index.js - the ncc-generated bundle of src/index.js. Wrong for the same reason, and it is a second thread for one issue because the generated bundle is inside the reviewed surface.
guidance_note: add the generated dist/ bundle to EXCLUDE_PATTERNS so no src finding can be re-raised against its compiled copy.

evidence: records.jsonl is written only by this same process's collector server (appendCollectorRecord), so a malformed line is not an external-input case and the residue is error-message quality, not a correctness hole. The reviewer cited [LAW:no-defensive-null-guards] - a law that argues against the guard it is demanding.
guidance_note: say at the parse site that a file is written only by this process, so a reviewer's boundary-input reflex does not fire on every JSON.parse.

evidence: The same JSON.parse claim as F7, on the generated dist/index.js:32170. F13 raises it a third time at the identical path and line, so one issue produced three threads in a single round.
guidance_note: excluding the generated bundle from the reviewed surface removes both the duplicate and the triplicate at once.

evidence: The finding's own second sentence retracts its first: it asserts the skip message prints when canApprove is true, then concedes 'the info message in the else branch is correct'. What is left is a rename suggestion (submitCleanReviewIfApproved), which the action's own reviewer prompt classes as a naming preference and forbids. The thread is still unresolved at merge.
The dist/index.js copy of F9's rename suggestion, with [LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow] attached to a function-naming preference. The name is unchanged at 28b275f and the thread is unresolved.

Verified in run() at 28b275f: reviewOctokit = getOctokit(reviewToken || token) and it is the octokit used for the REQUEST_CHANGES submission as well as the approval, so the README's 'when GITHUB_TOKEN cannot approve' is genuinely incomplete. It is a documentation nit rather than a defect, and it was never fixed - the README line is unchanged at merge.
guidance_note: when adding an optional credential, document every call it is wired into, not just the case that motivated it.

evidence: Same incompleteness as F11, in action.yml's input description. The reviewer cited [LAW:one-source-of-truth] on the wording while walking past the actual duplication it names: the token's description is written twice, in README.md and action.yml, and both were left stale.
guidance_note: an input's description that must be written in two files is one fact with two homes; state it once and have the other reference it.

evidence: The third thread for F7's JSON.parse point, at the same dist/index.js:32170 as F8 - the reviewer duplicated itself inside one round on one line. Same verdict as F7: the records file has a single in-process producer.

run() reads pullNumber and headSha from context.payload.pull_request, so on a non-pull_request event both are absent together and on a pull_request event head.sha is always present; the branch the reviewer imagines (right event, missing sha) is unreachable and the message is accurate. [LAW:comments-explain-why-only] governs comments, not error strings.
The dist/index.js duplicate of F14, wrong for the same reason: both fields come off the same optional payload object and cannot disagree.

There was a real position bug, but not the one described: GitHub counts every line after the FIRST hunk header, so the reviewer's proposed fix (count only lines starting with '+') would have shipped a worse defect. 28b275f instead introduced a patchPositions generator that treats only the first @@ as the baseline and counts later headers, which both the anchor table and the annotation now read - fixing the multi-hunk off-by-N without taking the advice.
guidance_note: derive an external protocol's numbering in one generator both consumers read, instead of two loops that independently re-derive it.

evidence: 28b275f changed only patchPositions/buildPatchAnchors/annotatePatchWithPositions, so the post-review-commit flag is a re-review of untouched code - submitCleanReview is unchanged since 2fc542e, before round 0. The shape does match [LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow], but the proposed fix is incoherent: the event is already findings.length > 0 ? 'REQUEST_CHANGES' : 'APPROVE', and canApprove gates token permission, not event type. The PR merged over this open CHANGES_REQUESTED thread with no reply.
guidance_note: when merging over an open blocking thread, record the rejection on the thread; a silently resolved thread leaves no evidence the claim was considered.

narrative: Four rounds, seventeen threads, and not one reply: every thread was resolved (or left open) without an answer, and code inspection at the merge commit shows twelve of the round-1 findings were never acted on. Round 0 approved the same submitCleanReview and readCollectedReview code that round 1 then flagged twelve times, and eight of those twelve threads are duplicates of four issues - because the generated dist/index.js bundle is inside the reviewed surface, and once (F8/F13) because the reviewer duplicated itself on an identical path:line. The one genuinely valuable finding, F16's position bug, arrived with a wrong diagnosis and a fix that would have shipped a defect; the agent found the real GitHub semantics itself and fixed it correctly. F17 was left open and the PR merged over a CHANGES_REQUESTED review.
guidance_observations: This PR predates the address-pr-reviews reply convention: sixteen of seventeen threads have no reply, so nothing records which findings were rejected on purpose and which were simply dropped.
Reviewing the ncc-generated dist/ bundle alongside src/ doubled every finding in this PR and is the single largest source of duplicate threads in the batch.

Round 0 approved code that round 1 flagged twelve times with no intervening change to it - the reviewer is non-deterministic across rounds on identical code, so an approval carries no information about a later round.

evidence: npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1 || die 'build failed. Run npm run build to see the error.' does discard the diagnostic the die message then tells the operator to go find; dropping 2>&1 is exactly right. The agent also drew the correct line around the fix, keeping 2>&1 on the boolean precondition probes (gh auth status, git ls-remote) whose stderr is noise.
guidance_note: suppress stdout only where stderr is the diagnostic the caller will need; reserve 2>&1 for probes whose result is a boolean.

narrative: One round, one accurate finding, one fix, merged nine minutes later. The reviewer found a genuine no-silent-failure hole in a release script and the agent both fixed it and explained why the sibling 2>&1 uses stay - a discriminating reply rather than a blanket sweep.
guidance_observations: A finding stated with the exact edit ('change X to Y') produced a one-round close; nothing in this PR needed a second round.

evidence: A .overloaded property bolted onto a generic Error is a discriminator the type system cannot see; replacing it with class OverloadError extends Error and dispatching on instanceof puts the discriminator in the type, which is what the cited law asks for. The reviewer's premise and its proposed mechanism were both right.
guidance_note: when an error needs a discriminator, introduce the error subclass at the point of classification rather than tagging a property onto a generic Error.

evidence: src/index.js is the action's own entry script - node dist/index.js, re-spawned as the MCP collector through the same path - and no module requires it, so there is no consumer API to widen and no drift cost. The repo does carry a test/ tree that imports these pure functions, so the exports are a verification seam, and [LAW:types-are-the-program] says nothing about export surface.
guidance_note: label a test-seam export as such at the export site, so a reviewer does not read it as a widened public API.

evidence: The finding text is the reviewer's own retraction - 'Withdrawn - runtime error classification via property flag is acceptable in JavaScript' - yet it was still submitted as a blocking inline request_change. The property it referred to was already gone, replaced by OverloadError under F1.

narrative: Three inline comments in round 0, of which one was real (the untyped .overloaded flag), one was a preference dressed as a type law (module.exports surface), and one was the reviewer posting its own withdrawal as a blocking comment. The agent fixed the real one, pushed back on the preference with an argument about what the file actually is, and noted the third was moot. Rounds 1 through 3 were re-reviews of the agent's own follow-up commits and found nothing.
guidance_observations: A retracted finding still arrived as a blocking inline comment and consumed a thread and a reply - the reviewer has no channel for withdrawing a request_change once emitted.
Three of the four rounds were triggered by the agent's own pushes and produced zero findings; each still cost a full model run.

evidence: In da43541 the delay is Math.min(err.retryAfterMs ?? backoff, budgetLeft) while the label tested only whether retryAfterMs was non-null, so a budget-capped wait printed '[Retry-After]' and the log named a constraint that had not decided anything. The reviewer's diagnosis was exact.
guidance_note: a label that names which of several inputs won must be derived from the comparison that selected the winner, not from the presence of one candidate.

evidence: The reviewer's replacement formula returns 'backoff' when retryAfterMs is null and the backoff exceeds budgetLeft, where 'budget' is the correct answer; the shipped hintOrBackoff <= budgetLeft ? (retryAfterMs !== null ? 'Retry-After' : 'backoff') : 'budget' is right in all three cases. The line exists only because it was written to close F1, and 40ec6d8 shows the agent had already self-corrected its own first attempt (delay === budgetLeft, which misreports on coincidental equality) before this round opened.
guidance_note: the first fix compared the post-cap result against the cap; compare the pre-cap candidate instead, so equal values do not misattribute the source.

narrative: Eight review rounds on a 57-line change, five of them clean approvals before the first finding appeared. Round 5's finding was real and precisely stated - the delay-source label was derived from the input rather than the winner. Round 7 then re-flagged the corrected line with a formula that was itself wrong for the null-hint case, and the agent's pushback traced the counterexample correctly. The one genuinely avoidable round is round 7, which exists because the F1 fix put a new expression on that line; the agent had already spotted and fixed its own coincidental-equality bug in that expression a commit earlier.
guidance_observations: Every push re-triggered a full review: five of eight rounds found nothing and existed only because the agent pushed a self-correction.

The agent's first fix for F1 was subtly wrong (delay === budgetLeft) and it caught that itself rather than the reviewer catching it - the self-correction commit is the cheapest round in this PR and the pattern worth encouraging.

evidence: DEFAULT_TOOL_NAMES in prompt.js restated the same MCP tool-name strings that TOOL_NAMES already owns in engine/claude-code.js, and run.js:150 always passes adapter.toolNames, so the default was both a second home for the fact and dead. Sharper still: b715049's own commit message says it hoisted TOOL_NAMES to remove a duplicate - and left this duplicate behind in the process.
guidance_note: a commit that consolidates a duplicated fact must delete the defaulted copy at the consumer and make the parameter required, or it just moves the duplicate.

evidence: In JavaScript the outer finally runs whenever the outer try block exits, an exception thrown from the inner finally included, so collector.dir is cleaned in every path and the reviewer's ordering premise is false. The flagged nested try/finally was introduced in b715049, not in the flagged commit 24ffe1d (which changed prompt.js and the materializeHome signature), so the post-review-commit flag points at the wrong change.
guidance_note: state the language guarantee a nested try/finally leans on in the comment beside it, so the guarantee is not re-litigated by a reader working from intuition.

narrative: Round 0 approved the PR with no findings; rounds 1 and 2 each produced one finding on code the agent added after that approval. F1 was a genuine one-source-of-truth violation that the agent's own de-duplication commit had created. F2 was a false claim about JavaScript's finally semantics, correctly refused. Neither finding was caused by a fix for a packet finding - both target code from b715049, a commit the agent pushed on its own initiative.
guidance_observations: Both findings landed on code added after the first approval, which means the value of round 0's approval was zero and each subsequent push bought a fresh full review.
The commit that fixed a duplication introduced a second one in another file - the sweep stopped at the file being edited.

evidence: The missing space in '{},makeStub()' is real but it is formatting in a test file, and the action's own reviewer prompt says not to request changes for style; [LAW:verifiable-goals] has nothing to say about whitespace. The reviewer's own summary calls it 'a formatting preference, not a LAW violation' and then blocks the PR on it anyway. Applying the one-character edit was cheaper than arguing.
guidance_note: run the repo formatter over test files before pushing, so a cosmetic diff cannot become a blocking round.

narrative: Five review rounds on a 478-line PR produced exactly one inline finding: a missing space between two arguments in a test file, filed under [LAW:verifiable-goals] and submitted as CHANGES_REQUESTED. The reviewer's own summary concedes it is a formatting preference and not a law violation in the same paragraph that blocks on it. Rounds 0, 1, 2 and 4 found nothing.
guidance_observations: The reviewer blocked a PR on whitespace while its prompt explicitly forbids style findings - the prompt's prohibition is not binding on the request_change tool, only on the model's judgment.
The round-4 summary raised a real observation (the early-return path calls submitReview without the new attributionFooter argument) as a non-blocking note, so it produced no thread and no follow-up.

evidence: Read at bc2eab2, the reviewed commit: peekConfigNames guarded only if (!raw.default), with no type check - the reviewer was right. The typeof raw.default !== 'string' guard first appears in f04d69b, the commit the agent pushed in response, and the String() cast the reply claims to have removed in 'this commit' actually survived until f30ae82. The reply's 'already fixed in the previous commit' is false on both counts, even though the code eventually landed correctly.
guidance_note: read the guard at the reviewed commit before replying 'already fixed'; a false already-fixed tells the reviewer nothing changed at exactly the moment something did.

evidence: BODY_DIRECTIVE_RE carries the i flag, and in ECMAScript /i case-folds character-class ranges, so [a-z0-9_.-] already matches 'MyConfig' - the uppercase claim is simply wrong. A narrower version of the asymmetry does survive the pushback: the label path applies no character restriction at all, so a config name containing a space or slash still parses from a label and not from the body directive.
guidance_note: when two input paths select the same value, run both through one name-validation rule instead of one regex and one prefix strip.

narrative: Round 0 approved; rounds 1 and 2 each found one thing. F1 was correct and the agent fixed it, but reported the fix as an already-existing guard - a claim the reviewed commit contradicts, and the second half of that reply (that the String() cast was removed in the response commit) was wrong too. F2 was a misreading of a regex flag, refused with a correct and checkable argument. The pattern across the two: the pushback was better evidenced than the acceptance.
guidance_observations: The 'already_fixed' reply shape is the one the reviewer cannot verify and the one this PR got wrong; it deserves the same evidence bar as a pushback.
Round 2's finding landed on a line the F1 response commit had edited for an unrelated reason, which is how a correct fix draws an unrelated wrong finding onto itself.

evidence: Line 50 reads model = ${q(INTERNAL_PROVIDER + '/' + config.model)} - the concatenation is the argument to the escaper, not a bypass of it - and TOML literal strings are single-quote delimited, so a backtick is an ordinary character that cannot change string type. The reviewer's own round-1 summary retracts the finding ('I submitted an incorrect change request based on a misreading - line 50 DOES properly apply q() escaping') while still submitting CHANGES_REQUESTED with it attached. The agent's closing [LAW:types-are-the-program] tag is the reviewer's token echoed onto a no-change resolution and argues nothing.
guidance_note: build an escaped external-format value in one helper that owns the whole field, so no call site can be misread as concatenating around the escaper.

narrative: Round 0 approved a 690-line adapter cleanly. Round 1 blocked on a single finding that the same review's summary explicitly retracts as a misreading - the reviewer knew the finding was wrong and shipped it as CHANGES_REQUESTED anyway. The agent refuted both halves of it (escaping placement, TOML backtick semantics) with specifics and merged.
guidance_observations: The reviewer's summary and its inline findings can contradict each other within one round, because retraction has no path back through the request_change channel once the tool has been called.
A round that costs a full model run and an agent reply to dispose of a finding the reviewer already knew was wrong is pure overhead.

evidence: Dropping env_key from a custom Codex provider without setting requires_openai_auth leaves Codex treating it as unauthenticated, so the saved credential is ignored - a real config defect in the PR's own new file. The agent applied the fix, verified live that codex exec completes a turn with it, and named the deeper cause (Codex 0.139 also ignores env_key on the Responses transport, so the credential now lives in CODEX_HOME/auth.json). The reviewer's [LAW:single-enforcer] tag does not fit an auth-wiring bug.
guidance_note: when swapping a provider's credential channel, run the engine once against the new config before opening the PR; unauthenticated is a silent failure mode, not a build error.

narrative: One accurate, high-value finding in round 0 - the new default-engine config would have shipped unauthenticated - fixed and live-verified in one round. The reviewer also disclosed, in both rounds, that it could not run the test suite because @actions/core was not installed in its workspace, so its verdict rests on reading alone.
guidance_observations: The reviewer cannot run this repo's tests (no node_modules in the review workspace) and says so in most rounds; every correctness verdict in this batch after PR 23 is read-only.
The law token on this finding was decorative - the defect was real, the cited law was not the one it violated, which means the token carries no signal about whether a finding is worth acting on.

evidence: if (!headRepo || !baseRepo) return true collapsed two different domain states into one answer: a deleted fork source, where 'fork' is correct, and a malformed payload, where skipping the review silently is the wrong outcome. The fix splits them so an absent base.repo throws and run.js surfaces it via setFailed. The original code's own comment cited [LAW:no-defensive-null-guards] to justify the collapse.
guidance_note: when one predicate returns the same answer for two inputs that mean different things, split them at write time - a comment defending the collapse is the tell that the enumeration was not done.

narrative: A single correct finding on a security-relevant classifier: the fork test treated a malformed PR payload as a fork and skipped the review silently. The agent accepted it and separated the two domain states properly rather than adding a guard. Notably the code being flagged carried an inline law citation arguing the merged branch was legitimate - the citation was wrong and the reviewer saw through it.
guidance_observations: An inline [LAW:...] citation in the code under review did not deter a correct finding, which is the right outcome; a law tag in the source is a claim, not a defense.

evidence: gpt-5.4-mini's cachedInput of 0.1875 is a 75%-discount outlier against the table's own gpt-5.5 (5.00 to 0.50) and gpt-5.4 (2.50 to 0.25) rows, which both use ten percent of input; the agent corrected it to 0.075 and realigned the two dependent test expectations. The external price itself cannot be re-verified from here, so the basis is the table's internal ratio invariant, which both parties reasoned from.
guidance_note: give a hand-maintained price table an invariant test (cachedInput equals ten percent of input) so a single mis-sourced row cannot enter unnoticed.

evidence: A null costUsd genuinely has two producers with different causes (codex: model absent from the price table; claude-code: envelope omitted total_cost_usd) and the warning hardcoded the codex one. The agent took 'carry the reason from the adapter' over 'branch on engine here' and made cost a discriminated value, which is the better of the two offered fixes. The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive: 68da4ce touched only src/usage.js, test/usage.test.js and dist/index.js - never src/run.js, where this warning lives, which came from the original commit a5d664b.
guidance_note: when one null value has two producers with different causes, have each producer name its own reason where it knows it, instead of a consumer re-deriving a cause it cannot see.

evidence: 616e15a - the F2 fix - introduced the {available:true, usd} cost shape in src/engine/claude-code.js, which is the exact line round 2 flagged, so this round exists because of that fix even though the overclaim it names predates it. The reviewer was right that the footer overclaimed precision and wrong about the remedy: every cost this action renders is a price-table-times-tokens estimate, so an 'exact' discriminant would be a state that never occurs, and marking every cost line 'est.' is strictly more correct than caveating only claude-code.
guidance_note: before adding a discriminator field, check whether both of its values ever occur; a fact that is invariantly true belongs in the renderer, not in the type.

narrative: The clearest fix-caused chain in the batch. F1's price correction was clean and self-contained. F2 targeted run.js code that predated the F1 fix, so the named-fix-commit flag is a false positive there. F3 is the real link: the discriminated cost value introduced to close F2 is what drew round 2's finding, and the underlying overclaim had been sitting in the code since round 0 without being seen. All three replies show a plan posted before the fix and a fix comment naming the commit and the test count, and in the two different-fix cases the agent's alternative was better reasoned than the proposal it declined.
guidance_observations: Restructuring a value's representation to close one finding re-exposes the whole value to the next round; finishing the representation in one pass (reason AND estimate-ness together) would have collapsed rounds 1 and 2 into one.
Every reply here posts a plan first and then a separate fixed-in-sha comment - the two-message shape makes the reasoning auditable and is why these threads can be graded without reading the code.

evidence: The agent reports verifying against opencode 1.1.40 that 'opencode run' reads the prompt from stdin when given no message positional, with the falsifiable detail that empty stdin errors 'You must provide a message or a command', and runEngine does pipe the full prompt to child.stdin; the adapter also completed a real end-to-end review this way. The reviewer re-asserted the same claim in round 1 with no evidence and no reference to the rebuttal. The verification is the agent's reported live run, not independently reproduced here.
guidance_note: when an undocumented CLI behavior is load-bearing, put the verification command and its observed output in the comment beside the spawn spec - this finding returned a second round without it.

evidence: A genuine isolation hole in a security boundary: the reviewer subprocess runs with cwd set to the reviewed repo, and opencode walks up from cwd loading ./opencode.json and .opencode/. The agent reproduced it by planting a hostile ./opencode.json that took over the run's model, then established that the reviewer's suggested --pure is not a real opencode flag and used the actual gate, OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG, with a test asserting it. The existing comment claimed isolation while covering only the global XDG config.
guidance_note: when isolating a spawned agent from an untrusted repo, cover project-level config discovery from cwd, not just the global config home, and prove it with a planted hostile config in a test.

narrative: Two findings in one round, one wrong and one excellent. The wrong one (prompt not passed on argv) was refused with a live check against opencode 1.1.40; the reviewer re-raised it verbatim in round 1 without engaging the rebuttal. The right one found a real prompt-injection surface - a reviewed repo could plant an ./opencode.json and take over the reviewer's model, permissions and MCP servers - and the agent's fix is better than the one suggested, because the suggested flag does not exist. Round 1 also raised a new unvalidated-provider-string finding that could not be anchored to a diff line, so it landed in the summary only and the PR merged with it unaddressed.
guidance_observations: A finding the reviewer cannot anchor to a changed line is emitted in the summary body, produces no thread, and therefore gets no plan, no fix, and no resolution - two such findings were lost at merge in this PR.
A pushback backed by a reproducible command did not stop the reviewer re-raising the identical claim next round; the reviewer does not read prior thread replies.

evidence: The premise checks out and the agent confirmed the specific mechanism: OpenCode's extractUsage sums tokens across every step_finish event, so tail-truncating the shared stdout buffer would undercount usage with no error, while codex (last turn.completed) and claude-code (single terminal envelope) are tail-safe. The agent declined both proposals with reasons - keeping full stdout reintroduces the unbounded-memory failure the cap exists for, and an adapter-specific retention window leaks usage knowledge into the generic spawn runner - and made the clip loud instead, with tests that the warning fires above the cap and not below.
guidance_note: when changing a shared buffer from fail-hard to truncate, enumerate every consumer of that buffer and state which are tail-safe before shipping the change.

narrative: The best single exchange in the batch. The reviewer found a real hole the PR itself introduced - truncating a shared stdout buffer breaks the one adapter that sums across the whole event stream - and offered two fixes, both worse than the problem. The agent verified the specific adapter claim, named why each proposal was wrong, and shipped a third option that keeps the bound and makes the loss announced. One round, closed.
guidance_observations: The finding that mattered here was about a consumer the change never touched; a change to a shared buffer's semantics needs a consumer sweep, and neither the original PR nor the first review prompt asks for one.

evidence: hostname.endsWith('anthropic.com') accepts notanthropic.com, so a lookalike endpoint would be classified as Anthropic and its Anthropic-priced cost rendered as real - a textbook enumeration gap in a classifier the PR was specifically written to tighten. The fix, host === 'anthropic.com' || host.endsWith('.anthropic.com'), closes it, with a lookalike regression test.
guidance_note: a domain-suffix check needs the dot boundary and the bare-domain case written together; endsWith(domain) is never the whole rule.

evidence: Verified at the reviewed commit 3e23f36: endpointHost is called only from costWarning (usage.js:115), and buildReviewFooter in run.js sends costWarning's text to core.warning while the posted footer comes from renderCostLine, which never calls endpointHost - so there is no review-comment sink for the raw baseUrl. baseUrl also comes from action inputs or the maintainer's committed config, and fork PRs are never reviewed, so it is not PR-controlled under the repo's own trust model.

narrative: One round, two findings, both engaged properly: an accurate enumeration gap in a host classifier that the agent fixed with a regression test, and a data-flow claim about untrusted text reaching the review comment that the agent traced to ground and refused. The refusal is checkable from the code and holds - endpointHost has exactly one caller and that caller's output only reaches the Actions log.
guidance_observations: Both findings targeted the same twenty-line function, and the one the agent had to refuse required tracing a value to its sink; a comment naming the sink at the function would have pre-empted it.

evidence: scripts/local-review.js ran fs.mkdtempSync and mutated RUNNER_TEMP at module top, so test/local-review.test.js importing parseArgs and formatReport performed filesystem IO and perturbed transcript discovery for anything that ran after; bbb848b moved all of it into main(). The fix is real, but the agent replied in a PR issue comment rather than on the thread, which is still unresolved.
guidance_note: keep a CLI's pure helpers importable - do temp-dir creation and env mutation inside main(), so helper tests import without world-effects.

evidence: The flag is the relocation false positive: if (!fs.existsSync(TRANSCRIPT_DIR)) return [] is byte-identical at 5f41c60, before the F1 fix, and bbb848b only turned the directory into a parameter. The finding itself stands - a diagnostic whose whole purpose is reporting what the engine did should not render an empty session list when transcript capture failed - and the agent neither replied nor fixed it; the PR merged with the thread open and the review still CHANGES_REQUESTED.
guidance_note: in a diagnostic tool, a missing input is a failed run, not an empty result - return-empty is the one shape that makes a broken diagnostic look successful.

narrative: Two accurate findings, one fixed and one abandoned. F1's import-time side effects were real and fixed properly, but the agent answered in a PR issue comment instead of on the thread, so the thread reads as ignored. F2 is correct and unanswered: the PR merged over an open CHANGES_REQUESTED review with a return-empty-on-missing-transcripts hole still in the diagnostic. Its post-review-commit flag is a false positive - the return-[] line predates the F1 fix and was only parameterized by it.
guidance_observations: Replying in an issue comment rather than on the thread leaves the thread unresolved and the review blocking, and makes the response invisible to any per-thread audit.
Merging over an unanswered blocking finding happened twice in this batch (PR 5 F17, PR 46 F2); in both cases the finding had substance.

evidence: [ "$HEAD_VERSION" = "$BASE_VERSION" ] rejects only equality, so 1.21.2 to 1.20.0 passes as a valid 'bump' - the enforcement encoded not-equal where the rule is strictly-greater. The agent took the theorem and refused the mechanism because semver is not a dependency of this project (deps are @actions/core, @actions/github and yaml), so the suggested node -e require('semver') would have reddened every PR, and wrote a pure-node numeric x.y.z compare instead, verifying downgrade, equal and increase.
guidance_note: write the enforcement as the rule states it (strictly greater), not as the negation of the single failure you happened to picture (not equal).

evidence: The same git rev-parse --verify refs/tags/$VERSION predicate ran inline in release.yml and again inside release.sh, so one rule had two implementations. The agent took the reviewer's exact proposal - an --if-untagged flag on release.sh - and deleted the inline gate, which also closed the coverage mismatch the reviewer noted in passing, because skip_or_die wraps release.sh's local AND remote tag checks while the inline gate only checked local.
guidance_note: an inline comment that names a duplication and argues it is acceptable ('two questions, one predicate') is the signal to remove the duplication, not to ship it.

narrative: Two accurate, high-value findings in one round, both closed in one fix commit. F1 caught an enforcement script that permitted the exact thing it existed to prevent; the agent took the theorem and rejected the mechanism for a concrete reason (semver is not a dependency, so the suggested check would have failed at require time). F2 caught a predicate with two homes, and the agent took the reviewer's design verbatim, which also fixed a coverage gap the reviewer had only mentioned as an aside.
guidance_observations: This is the review the whole pipeline is for: two real defects in CI-enforcement code, both found before merge, both closed in one round.

The replacement version compare is a numeric x.y.z split with no prerelease handling; it is correct for the versions this repo uses today but would misjudge 1.22.0-rc.1, and nothing in the tests pins that.

evidence: The PR added engines.node '>=24' while CONTRIBUTING.md line 21 still said 'Node.js 20+', so the same fact had two disagreeing homes and the contradiction was introduced by this diff. The agent converged upward to match action.yml's using: node24 rather than weakening engines to >=20, which is the right direction because action.yml is the runtime that actually decides.
guidance_note: when adding a field that restates an existing fact, grep for every other place that fact is written and update them in the same commit.

evidence: The identical engines.node versus CONTRIBUTING.md contradiction as F1, posted a second time on the adjacent line of the same hunk (package.json:12 and :13), against the reviewer's own instruction to file one comment per distinct issue. One CONTRIBUTING.md edit resolved both threads and the agent posted the same plan and fix text to each.

narrative: One real finding - the PR introduced a Node-version contradiction between package.json engines and CONTRIBUTING.md - filed twice on adjacent lines of one hunk, so the agent wrote the same plan and the same fix comment on two threads. The fix was right and picked the correct direction of convergence. The round-0 and round-1 summaries also listed several accurate pre-existing documentation gaps (missing zai provider in the README tables, GITHUB_TOKEN absent from the inputs table, LICENSE holder mismatch, v-prefix tag inconsistency) that produced no threads and no follow-up.
guidance_observations: The reviewer filed one issue as two findings on two lines of the same hunk, doubling the agent's reply cost for no information.
Accurate pre-existing findings surface only in the summary body, so they generate no thread, no plan and no fix - the review's most reusable output is the part with no mechanism behind it.
